title: Eight Children in a Three-Bedroom House: How Makini School Began
dek: In 1978 a Nairobi bank manager and her engineer husband opened a nursery school in their own home, paid for from their savings, while both kept their day jobs.

story.event: Opening a nursery school with eight children in the family's three-bedroom house in Nairobi
story.summary: In 1978 Mary Okelo, then manager of Barclays' Westlands branch in Nairobi, and her husband Pius opened a nursery school with eight children in their three-bedroom house, funded from savings, because they could not afford land. Named Riara Gardens Academy and later Makini, it was run as a side business by a senior teacher and grew a class at a time at parents' request. In 1992 Okelo left her international banking work to run it full-time.
paragraphs: In 1977 Barclays gave Mary Okelo its Westlands branch in Nairobi, which, she later told Harvard Business School, was losing money and had very low staff morale. She was the first African woman to manage a branch for the bank. Getting there had cost her: in 1973 she turned down a branch in Nakuru because her children were small and her husband, Pius, lectured in Nairobi, and waited four years for another promotion.

Around then, by her account in a 2002 Columbia Business School case, she took to visiting a friend who had opened one of Kenya's first private primary schools. "I used to go to her school to get away from banking," she said. The friend told her: "Since you love children so much, why don't you start a school? It's a good business." The Okelos were also watching the public system strain. Kenya's population was growing, she reckoned, at about five per cent a year, the government was not building enough schools, and classes were reaching seventy children. A teacher, she said, "can't mark seventy essays in an evening."

Land in Nairobi was scarce and costly. "That's why we started in our own house, because we couldn't afford to buy land," she said. In 1978 the couple opened a nursery school in their three-bedroom home with eight children, paid for from their savings. It was called Riara Gardens Academy at first and was meant as a side business: she stayed at the bank, Pius had just left university teaching to start an engineering consultancy, and a senior teacher ran the school day to day. They aimed for about twenty-five children per teacher instead of seventy. Later they borrowed from Barclays, offering the house as security.

Parents kept asking for another class so their children need not move on; they told the Okelos they were not leaving, Pius recalled. Renamed Makini in 1981, the school moved into its own building in 1982 and added the last primary year in 1985. By the Columbia case writers' count it had about 400 pupils by 1989. In 1992, having to choose between her international banking work and the school, Mary chose the school and ran it full-time. By 1997, the case says, its three primary schools taught about 1,600 children.

quote.text: With that gentleness I can be bold; with that economy I can be liberal; shrinking from taking precedence of others, I can become a vessel of the highest honour.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi pairs economy with liberality: what you hold back is what lets you give freely later. The Okelos' thrift, a school in their own house paid for from savings, made room for classes of twenty-five instead of seventy, and a love of children gave a busy banker the nerve to begin.

reflection: Okelo did not wait for land she could not afford. She started in the house she already had, with eight children and her savings, and kept her job while the idea proved itself. The school grew because parents asked it to, one class at a time.

Notice, too, where the idea came from: afternoons at a friend's school, taken to get away from banking. What you turn to for relief on hard days can tell you something about yourself. It need not become a business. Sometimes it is simply what keeps you whole while the main work goes on.
invitation: Think of the place you go, or the thing you do, when you need an hour away from work. Make time for it once this week, and do not ask it to be useful.

research_notes: Where the school began: Okelo herself (HBS 2015; How we made it in Africa 2013) says their three-bedroom house; Business Daily (2011) says a home backyard; Business Today (2018) says the colonial bungalow where the founders lived. The story uses her own 'three-bedroom house'. All sources give eight children and 1978; Business Today adds February 1978. 'First' claims differ: Columbia and Paukwa say first African woman to be a (Barclays) branch manager, Kenyans.co.ke and Wikipedia say first woman bank manager in Kenya; the story uses the narrower Barclays claim. Pupil numbers: the 400 (1989) and 1,600 (1997) figures come only from the 2002 Columbia case and are attributed to it; Business Daily in 2011 said only 'more than 1,000 students'. The five per cent population growth is Okelo's own recollection and is attributed. Funding: the slate said bootstrapped; it began on savings in the family house, with Barclays loans secured on the house later (the HBS transcript does not date the first loan), and no outside equity until the 2018 sale, so 'bootstrapped' is kept. The sale is left out because sources disagree: Business Today (2018) says Schole acquired all the shares, while Kenyans.co.ke (2021) says she sold a 71 per cent stake for nearly Ksh1 billion to Schole and ADvTECH. The friend's advice is quoted as Okelo reported it to the Columbia case writers; the case's ellipsis after 'to get away from banking' is not reproduced. The HBS profile page blocks automated requests, so the transcript is cited from its Wayback Machine copy. The Laozi passage concerns the sage's three treasures; it is applied by analogy.
